newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Overweight HK with eye on Bangkok, Seoul - Merrill.
newsitem.headline: Overweight HK with eye on Bangkok, Seoul - Merrill.

text.p: Investors should continue to remain overweight in Hong Kong equities next year, with Thailand and South Korea seen as potential dark horses in the second half of 1997, Merrill Lynch said on Tuesday.

At a presentation of Merrill Lynch's Asia-Pacific outlook, regional strategist Pauline Gately said declining U.S. bond yields in the first half of 1997 should stimulate interest in Asian markets, although the magnitude of the boost was unclear.
Hong Kong's stocks have moved up 28 percent this year and should continue rising, she said.
"We think we'll see follow-through performance in 1997," she said. "We feel there is solid upside in Hong Kong."

As well as declining bond yields, improved liquidity in China and an upbeat prognosis for earnings and the economy pointed to an overweighting in Hong Kong shares, Merrill said in a report dated December 10.
It forecast 15 percent earnings per share growth for Hang Seng Index companies and fair valuation for the blue chip barometer at 15,000 points.

Property and bank counters were behind the Hang Seng's push to record highs over the course of 1996 but Merrill said investors should also look at media and hotel stocks as well as the red-chip firms based in Hong Kong but focused on China.
Merrill said it felt comfortable with the liquidity situation in China and that official policy tools were being used effectively. Any benefits would spill over into Hong Kong, said Gately.

She said Merrill was looking for a pick-up in regional export growth, particularly in China, after a deterioration during 1996. Current account improvements also were needed in many countries in the region.

Two laggards -- Thailand and South Korea -- also topped Merrill's list of favourites. While neither market was for "the faint-hearted", Merrill said both were poised for a cyclical rebound in the second half of next year.
High gearing and relaxed monetary policy were among the benefits in both countries but there needed to be improvement in the current account picture, Gately said.
South Korea had been hurt by global price pressure on semiconductors and a "problem of inventory overhang", but Gately said she expected improvements in the second quarter.

The main factors to watch in South Korea, she said, were labour law reform to increase flexibility in redeploying workers and financial deregulation to trim the disparity between local and outside interest rates.
In Thailand, Gately said the political backdrop was "the critical issue to watch in 1997".

She said considerations for investors included return on equity which was "not that attractive", allocation of assets into projects that were "not really good investments" and the fragile position of the new coalition government.
"Possible catalysts for a better market include: current account deficit reduction, monetary leniency and relatively undemanding valuations outside of the financial sector," Merrill said.

Thailand's economic growth would be slower in 1997 than the expected 6.7 percent this year and the 8.6 percent of 1995, Gately said. But a drop of 120-150 basis points in Thai interest rates would bring out domestic investors, she added.
